source.title: Approaching Backpropagation Accuracy with Weight Perturbation on MNIST

record.tranche_reason: Tests the effect of batch size, training duration, and stabilization on MNIST accuracy, but refines the general claim: near-BP performance is attainable only for the shallow configuration at very high training exposure, while deeper tested configurations remain below BP within the reported budgets. The finite-horizon argument is theoretical, not an empirical result.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own WP and BP results on MNIST. Results quoted from Züge et al. and other prior work are excluded. Figure curves are described approximately in Results; dashed curve extensions are not measured continuations. The study does not test random-label memorization or natural-label generalization under the same recipe.
record.test_reason: The epoch-indexed shallow-network comparison bears on V5: on MNIST, weight perturbation with batch 4,000 attains higher test accuracy than batch 10,000 within the displayed matched exposure range. A different training method does not itself exclude this image-classifier batch-size result. Equal-update comparisons and WP–BP comparisons do not test the fixed-epoch claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: shallow WP reaches approximately 97% MNIST test accuracy after extensive large-batch training, near an early BP reference of 97.5–98%, with substantially slower learning. Deeper tested configurations do not establish BP parity. The finite-horizon approximation is conditional theory, not an empirical accuracy or efficiency guarantee.
record.recipe_differences: Uses simultaneous Gaussian weight perturbation rather than the claim's standard gradient methods; the empirical setting is fully connected MNIST and the main comparisons vary batch size, update/epoch budget, and stabilization.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size and whether results are indexed by updates or nominal epochs change the comparison; depth affects stability and attainable accuracy within the studied budgets; decreasing learning rate and increasing population averaging stabilize deeper WP training.

fits_no_version.finding: Extended large-batch WP approaches an early BP accuracy reference in the shallow network, but costs far more exposure; deeper WP remains unstable or below BP-comparable accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight perturbation can approach BP accuracy on shallow fully connected MNIST networks with substantial training, while efficiency and deeper-network stability remain constraints.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal update counts, batches 4,000–10,000 approach similar accuracy near 97%, while batches 1,000 and 2,000 remain lower.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The apparent batch-size advantage in shallow MNIST WP depends on whether training is compared by updates or data exposure.

fits_no_version.finding: Learning-rate reduction and averaging independent perturbations stabilize deeper WP configurations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reducing update variability can improve deep weight-perturbation trainability without establishing BP-level accuracy.

record.code_released: no; underlying run logs and training code are not distributed with this article
record.problems: Empirical results are derived from the author's 2023 master's thesis rather than newly performed experiments; underlying code and run logs are not distributed. Several learning-curve values are approximate textual descriptions or figure-only; deeper-network population and learning-rate results lack numerical accuracy values. Comparisons to BP use different settings and budgets, and the long-training BP protocol is stated not to be recommended.
record.rows_left_out: No separate numeric rows for individual curve points were recoverable from Figure 3; the panels provide curves without textual point values, so each batch and budget view is represented once as figure-only. The dashed B = 10,000 deep-network extension in Figure 2 is explicitly not a measured continuation and is not recorded as a result.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-versus-random-label held-out performance under the same recipe.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.

Language models, gradient-trained classifiers' batch penalties, a quantified critical batch size, and controlled demonstrations that longer training, warmup, scaling, normalization, or regularization remove a fixed-epoch penalty.
Dropout, training-set-size dependence, and dropout/weight-decay removal with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation or ranking against generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus removing equal numbers of random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The record incorrectly excludes all of V5 merely because WP differs from standard gradient training. Its epoch-indexed comparison directly measures the batch-size behavior V5 names. Only the explicitly stated batch 4,000 versus 10,000 ranking supports a verdict; equal-update endpoints and WP–BP comparisons cannot supply additional fixed-epoch evidence. Figure artwork was not available beyond the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization, chance-level test accuracy on random labels, and same-recipe comparison with natural labels.
No width sweep around the interpolation threshold or test-error behavior beyond the width needed for zero training error.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.

No large-batch versus small-batch comparison under a matched fixed epoch budget against the claim's listed models and recipes; the paper reports MNIST WP comparisons indexed by updates and epochs, plus a separate ten-epoch WP/BP comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or other measured generalization-gap predictor.
No removal of memorized training examples.

relationships.condition: Shallow fully connected MNIST network trained with weight perturbation; batch 10,000 versus 4,000 at matched nominal epoch exposure in the displayed range.
relationships.reason: Section 3.2 explicitly reports higher test accuracy for batch 4,000 than 10,000 in the epoch-indexed comparison (R11, R13); the difference is qualitative and unquantified.
relationships.display_finding: The study reports higher test accuracy with the smaller batch at matched nominal epoch exposure, but this qualitative comparison remains unverified.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
